title: Commodity hedging
subtitle: Weekly note for corporate hedging conversations: energy, metals, grains
headline: Week of 24 November 2026. Backwardation in Brent Crude, WTI Crude, Aluminium, Soybeans; contango in Natural Gas, Copper, Gold, Silver, Wheat, Corn. Realized vol is high against five years in Brent Crude, WTI Crude, Copper, Aluminium, Gold, Silver and low in no market: that is where option hedges are dear and cheap.

sections.title: Energy: what a hedge locks in, and what optionality costs
paragraphs: Brent Crude: backwardation, BZZ27 15.5% below BZF27. A producer selling 11 months forward locks in 15.5% less than the front; a consumer buying forward pays 15.5% less.
WTI Crude: backwardation, CLZ27 11.8% below CLF27. A producer selling 11 months forward locks in 11.8% less than the front; a consumer buying forward pays 11.8% less.
Natural Gas: contango, NGZ27 16.5% above NGZ26. A consumer buying 12 months forward pays 16.5% more than the front; a producer selling forward locks in 16.5% more.

Brent Crude: realized vol 60%, 91st percentile of five years. Options-based hedges (puts, collars) are expensive against history; forwards and swaps carry no vol premium. Implied vol is estimated at about 65%: on Bloomberg history since 2015, implied has run 1.08 times realized, with a typical error of 5 points. WTI Crude: realized vol 51%, 83rd percentile of five years. Options-based hedges (puts, collars) are expensive against history; forwards and swaps carry no vol premium. Implied vol, which is what an option actually costs, is 49%: close to what has been realized (-1.2 points). Natural Gas: realized vol 76%, 63rd percentile of five years, in line with history.

sections.title: Metals: what a hedge locks in, and what optionality costs
paragraphs: Copper: contango, HGZ27 6.6% above HGZ26. A consumer buying 12 months forward pays 6.6% more than the front; a producer selling forward locks in 6.6% more.

Aluminium: backwardation, ALIM27 4.6% below ALIZ26. A producer selling 6 months (the furthest contract on the free feed) forward locks in 4.6% less than the front; a consumer buying forward pays 4.6% less.
Gold: contango, GCZ27 5.7% above GCZ26. A consumer buying 12 months forward pays 5.7% more than the front; a producer selling forward locks in 5.7% more.
Silver: contango, SIZ27 5.0% above SIZ26. A consumer buying 12 months forward pays 5.0% more than the front; a producer selling forward locks in 5.0% more.

Copper: realized vol 31%, 82nd percentile of five years. Options-based hedges (puts, collars) are expensive against history; forwards and swaps carry no vol premium. Aluminium: realized vol 31%, 85th percentile of five years. Options-based hedges (puts, collars) are expensive against history; forwards and swaps carry no vol premium. Gold: realized vol 34%, 96th percentile of five years. Options-based hedges (puts, collars) are expensive against history; forwards and swaps carry no vol premium. Implied vol, which is what an option actually costs, is 34%: close to what has been realized (-0.8 points). Silver: realized vol 56%, 93rd percentile of five years. Options-based hedges (puts, collars) are expensive against history; forwards and swaps carry no vol premium.

sections.title: Agriculture: what a hedge locks in, and what optionality costs
paragraphs: Wheat: contango, ZWZ27 11.7% above ZWZ26. A consumer buying 12 months forward pays 11.7% more than the front; a producer selling forward locks in 11.7% more.
Corn: contango, ZCZ27 10.5% above ZCZ26. A consumer buying 12 months forward pays 10.5% more than the front; a producer selling forward locks in 10.5% more.
Soybeans: backwardation, ZSX27 3.8% below ZSF27. A producer selling 10 months forward locks in 3.8% less than the front; a consumer buying forward pays 3.8% less.

Wheat: realized vol 24%, 25th percentile of five years, in line with history. Corn: realized vol 21%, 51st percentile of five years, in line with history. Soybeans: realized vol 17%, 46th percentile of five years, in line with history.

paragraphs: Contracts closest to 6 and 12 months after the front; gas and grains compare the same season. Where the free feed stops before 12 months, the shape is read on the furthest contract.

paragraphs: Realized vol of the front-month series over 21 sessions, with its percentile over one and five years. Implied only where CBOE publishes it.

sections.title: How the free contracts track the European benchmarks
paragraphs: Measured once on Bloomberg history, weekly returns since November 2021. A ratio above 1 means the free contract is more volatile than the benchmark a European client hedges.

method: Talking points rank markets by how far their 12-month curve or their realized-vol percentile sits from normal. Context for client conversations, not a recommendation.
caveats: Free data: Yahoo Finance closes of NYMEX, COMEX and CBOT futures. Copper and aluminium are COMEX contracts, not LME; Brent is the NYMEX last-day financial contract. No TTF, power, coal, softs or pulp on the free feed.

Implied vol history exists only for WTI (OVX) and gold (GVZ). Brent's implied vol is estimated from realized with a ratio calibrated on Bloomberg history (typical error about 5 points, much more in stress); elsewhere the realized-vol percentile stands in for what options cost, which holds only if implied tracks realized.
The free contracts are US benchmarks: Henry Hub barely tracks European gas (TTF), and COMEX copper and CBOT wheat are more volatile than their LME and Euronext counterparts (see the table above).
The front-month series rolls from contract to contract, so weekly and monthly moves include roll gaps.

Curves come from listed contracts only (12 to 13 months out, fewer for grains and aluminium), not from swap curves. Deferred metal contracts trade thinly, so intermediate points can be noisy; the 12-month comparison uses the same delivery month a year later, usually the most liquid.

calculator.note: Black-76 on the future, one flat vol for every strike and tenor, option expiry approximated to the 20th of the month before delivery (Brent: two months before). A desk prices off the smile: puts would come out dearer and the free cap of a collar lower. Indicative, not a quote.
